subChunks.title: Partial, Expression, and Hash Indexes
subChunks.hookHtml: Beyond basic B-tree indexes lie specialised index types that solve problems the standard approach cannot — partial indexes, expression indexes, hash indexes, and BRIN for sequential data.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Partial index — index only some rows

-- Only index active users (90% are inactive — no benefit indexing them):
CREATE INDEX idx_users_active_email
  ON users (email)
  WHERE is_active = TRUE;

-- The query must include the same condition:
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'x@y.com' AND is_active = TRUE;
-- Uses idx_users_active_email (small, fast)
-- A query without WHERE is_active = TRUE does NOT use this index

Partial indexes are smaller and faster than full-column indexes when queries consistently filter to a subset of rows.

Expression index (functional index)

-- Case-insensitive email search:
CREATE INDEX idx_users_lower_email ON users (LOWER(email));

-- Query must use the same expression:
SELECT * FROM users WHERE LOWER(email) = LOWER($1);
-- Uses the expression index

Hash index

CREATE INDEX idx_hash ON sessions (session_token) USING HASH;

Hash indexes: faster for equality queries (=), not usable for ranges (<, BETWEEN), smaller than B-tree. PostgreSQL now WAL-logs them (safe in PG10+). Use for long-string equality lookups like tokens or UUIDs.

BRIN (Block Range Index)

CREATE INDEX idx_events_brin ON events (created_at) USING BRIN;

BRIN stores min/max values per disk block range. Tiny (kilobytes on billion-row tables). Efficient for append-only, naturally ordered columns like timestamps. Terrible for random-access columns.

storyBeats.text: A 500M-row events table. The timestamp column is indexed — but the index is 40GB and still slow for point-in-time queries.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: BRIN stores block-level min/max — kilobytes on a billion rows. It works because events are inserted in timestamp order: the blocks themselves contain roughly chronological data. For a random column with values scattered across blocks, BRIN is useless. For timestamps, it is magic.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Index type selection

For each column and query pattern, recommend the optimal index type and justify it:

  1. users.email — equality lookups only, case-insensitive
  2. orders.status — only 'pending' orders are queried by the processing service (95% are 'completed')
  3. events.created_at — time-range queries on an append-only table with 2B rows
  4. sessions.token — 256-char UUID-like string, equality only
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Expression index: CREATE INDEX ON users (LOWER(email)); — B-tree on the lowercased value supports case-insensitive equality efficiently. Queries must use WHERE LOWER(email) = LOWER($1).

2. Partial index: CREATE INDEX ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'; — Only pending orders are queried; 95% of rows are excluded from the index, making it tiny and fast. Queries must include AND status = 'pending'.

3. BRIN index: CREATE INDEX ON events (created_at) USING BRIN; — Events are inserted in timestamp order. BRIN stores min/max per block. On 2B rows, the index might be 1MB vs 40GB for a B-tree. Slightly less precise than B-tree but acceptable for time-range filters.

4. Hash index: CREATE INDEX ON sessions (token) USING HASH; — Long token strings with equality-only queries. Hash indexes are more compact than B-tree for string keys and faster for pure equality lookups.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Explain when a partial index is more appropriate than a full-column index, and describe the query pattern required to use a partial index effectively.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
A partial index is better when queries consistently filter to a small, well-defined subset of rows — typically a status or active/inactive boolean.

Example: soft-deletes. 99% of users have deleted_at IS NULL. A partial index on users(email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL covers essentially all active user queries while being 99% smaller than a full-table index on email.

Required query pattern: the WHERE clause in the query must include the same condition as the index's WHERE clause. WHERE email = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL uses the partial index. WHERE email = $1 alone does NOT — the planner cannot guarantee the index only covers the right rows.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain BRIN indexes: what they store, why they are tiny, when they work well, and when they fail.

options: An index that only covers rows satisfying a specified WHERE condition
An index covering only some columns of the table
An index with less precision than a full B-tree
A temporary index that expires after a session
questions.answer: An index that only covers rows satisfying a specified WHERE condition
questions.explanation: A partial index includes only rows where a predicate is true. CREATE INDEX ... WHERE status = 'pending' builds an index containing only pending rows — smaller, faster, and only usable by queries that filter on that condition.

questions.prompt: For what use case is a HASH index superior to B-tree?
options: Long-string equality lookups (UUIDs, tokens) where range queries are never needed
Any equality query — HASH is always faster than B-tree
questions.answer: Long-string equality lookups (UUIDs, tokens) where range queries are never needed
questions.explanation: HASH indexes use O(1) hash lookups for equality — faster than B-tree's O(log n) for pure equality. They are smaller for long string keys. Trade-off: they do not support range queries, ORDER BY, or prefix scans.

questions.prompt: A BRIN index on created_at works well when data is inserted in timestamp order. Why does it fail for a randomly-assigned UUID column?
options: BRIN stores min/max per disk block — random UUIDs distribute all possible values across every block, so the min/max range is always [MIN_UUID, MAX_UUID], matching everything
BRIN requires a monotonic sequence to compile
UUID columns require Hash indexes exclusively
questions.answer: BRIN stores min/max per disk block — random UUIDs distribute all possible values across every block, so the min/max range is always [MIN_UUID, MAX_UUID], matching everything
questions.explanation: BRIN works because naturally-ordered data (timestamps) means each disk block holds a narrow value range. Random UUIDs mix all value ranges in every block — BRIN's min/max spans the full UUID space, so every query matches every block. B-tree is required for random UUID columns.

questions.prompt: When is an expression index (functional index) necessary?
options: When queries filter on a function applied to a column — e.g. WHERE LOWER(email) = $1 — because a standard index on email cannot be used
Whenever a column is used in a function anywhere in the query
For all computed columns in SELECT
When a column is frequently updated
questions.answer: When queries filter on a function applied to a column — e.g. WHERE LOWER(email) = $1 — because a standard index on email cannot be used
questions.explanation: A regular index on email stores original-case values. WHERE LOWER(email) = $1 applies a function, breaking index usage. An expression index on LOWER(email) stores pre-computed lowercase values — the query matches the index structure exactly.
